unit.title: Draw and interpret sketches and simple drawings

summary: This unit teaches you to read the drawings you are given and to make clear, dimensioned sketches of your own. You will learn the kinds of drawings, the title block, lines, scales, orthographic views, isometric and oblique pictures, sections, dimensions, tolerances and symbols, and how to read electrical and building layout plans. You will also learn to sketch an object so that someone else could make it, to work out cut lengths from a drawing, and what to do when a drawing is unclear or wrong.

blocks.p: Drawings are the language of the trades. A drawing tells you what to make or install, how big, from what, where and how many, without a single spoken word. A sketch lets you pass that information on: to a customer, a supervisor or the workshop.

**Who it is for:** this unit is shared by the Welding and Fabrication and the Electrical Installation programmes at Level 2. Welders read fabrication drawings of brackets, frames, gates and grills; electricians read layout plans and circuit and wiring diagrams. Both must sketch existing items and new ideas clearly, and both must spot when a drawing is wrong or out of date.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Tell detail, assembly, layout, circuit and wiring drawings apart, and say what each is for.
Read the title block and notes
Find the title, number, revision, date, scale, projection, units, tolerances, material and quantity.
Say what each type of line shows, and work out real sizes from a scale.
Understand front, plan and end views in first and third angle projection, hidden detail and sectional views.
Read and sketch isometric and oblique views.
Find sizes, hole details and limits, and read common abbreviations and welding and electrical symbols.
Measure an object and make a neat, dimensioned freehand sketch in orthographic and isometric views.
Work out cut lengths and quantities, check the drawing against the real site, report problems and look after drawings.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on types of drawing, title blocks and revisions, scales, lines, orthographic and pictorial views, dimensions and tolerances, symbols and abbreviations, sections, electrical and welding drawings, sketching and problems with drawings.
A **written paper** with short answers (abbreviations, scale sums, names of drawings, lines and equipment) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks**: measuring and sketching a workshop item in orthographic and isometric views, and reading a sheet-metal drawing, then building a full-size card model of the part.

blocks.note: A drawing question is often a small sum. Write down the scale or the sizes, work it out, then ask yourself: does that answer make sense for a real gate, room or bracket?
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Kinds of drawings and the drawing sheet

head: Drawing
What it shows
Used by
rows: All the information needed to make a part or product: views, sizes, tolerances, material, finish, quantity
One single part, with all its sizes
How all the parts fit together, with a parts list; often few sizes
A welded item: parts, sizes, joints and welding symbols
A building or room seen from above, with walls, doors, windows and the positions of fittings
How the parts of a circuit are connected to work, using symbols; not where they are in the building
How each wire is connected to the terminals of the equipment
Electricians wiring a panel, motor or appliance
The main parts of a system as labelled boxes joined by lines
A quick drawing made by hand without instruments, with sizes added
Measuring up, ideas, passing on information
The flat shape that is cut and then folded or rolled to make a sheet-metal part

blocks.p: Drawings are made on **A-size** sheets. Each size is half the one above it, so two A4 sheets make one A3.
The **title block**, usually in the bottom right-hand corner, holds the facts about the drawing. **Read it first**, before you look at the views.

head: Item
Why it matters
rows: Make sure it is the right drawing for the job
Revision letter or number, and date
Make sure it is the latest issue
How the drawing size compares with the real size
First or third angle: where each view is placed
How far any size may vary unless another tolerance is written beside it
What to make it from and how to finish it (some drawings put these in the notes)
Who is responsible for the drawing
For example "Sheet 2 of 3": make sure you have every sheet

ul: **Revisions:** each time a drawing is changed it gets a new revision letter or number (Rev A, Rev B …) and date. A revision table on the sheet lists what changed. Always work from the **latest** revision.
**Parts list (bill of materials):** on an assembly drawing, a table giving each part's mark number, name, quantity, size and material.
**Notes:** general instructions such as the finish, weld sizes not shown, or "remove all sharp edges".
Most drawings today are made with **CAD** (computer-aided design) software; the rules for reading them are the same as for hand drawings.

For hand drawing and sketching: pencils (a hard **2H** for light construction lines, a softer **HB** for outlines and lettering), eraser, sharpener, grid paper, a drawing board with a T-square, **set squares** (45° and 30°/60°), a **compass** for circles and arcs, a protractor and a scale rule.

head: Line
Looks like
Shows
rows: Dimension lines, extension (projection) lines, leader lines, hatching on sections
Hidden outlines and edges you cannot see from that side
Long dashes with short dashes (or dots) between
Centre lines of holes and round parts; lines of symmetry; pitch circles
Chain line, thick at the ends and corners, with arrows and letters
A chain line made bold at each end
A cutting plane: where a section is taken, and which way it is viewed
A break: where part of a long object is left out, or a part view ends

blocks.note: On a development (flat pattern), fold lines must look different from cut lines. Many drawings show fold or bend lines as thin chain lines with a note such as "FOLD 90° UP". Check the drawing's notes or key.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **scale** compares the size on the drawing with the real size. It is written as a ratio, **drawing : real**.

head: Scale
Meaning
Typical use
rows: Reduction: the drawing is 2, 5, 10 or 20 times smaller than the real object
Enlargement: the drawing is 2, 5 or 10 times bigger

head: To find the real size
Do this
Example
rows: Multiply the drawing size by n
At 1:20, 65 mm on the drawing is 65 × 20 = 1300 mm
37 mm on the plan is 3700 mm = 3.7 m
Divide the drawing size by n
At 5:1, 60 mm on the drawing is 60 ÷ 5 = 12 mm

blocks.p: Choose the scale that makes the views fit the sheet clearly, with room for dimensions, notes and the title block. A gate 2400 mm wide drawn at 1:10 is 240 mm wide: it fits across an A3 sheet (420 mm) with room to spare, but would leave too little room on A4. At 1:20 it is 120 mm, small enough for A4. A clip 15 mm wide is better drawn at 2:1 or 5:1, so its details can be seen.

blocks.note: **Never measure a drawing with a rule to find a size.** Photocopies and prints shrink or stretch, and parts of a drawing are not always drawn exactly to scale. Work from the **written dimensions**. If a size you need is missing, ask: do not scale it. "NTS" means not to scale.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Orthographic projection, hidden detail and sections

blocks.p: An **orthographic** drawing shows an object as two or more flat views, each seen straight on from one direction. Each view shows the true shape and size of the faces that are square to it. One view cannot show every size and shape, so several are used.

head: View
Seen from
Shows
rows: Length and height; usually the view that shows the most about the shape

ul: The views **line up**: the plan sits directly in line with the front view (same length), and the end view in line with it (same height). Thin projection lines carry sizes from one view to the next.
Use only the views needed. A flat plate may need one view and a note of its thickness; a bracket usually needs two or three.

blocks.h: First angle and third angle projection

head: Point
First angle
Third angle
rows: Drawn on the **right** of the front view
Drawn on the **left** of the front view
Each view is drawn on the side **opposite** to the side it is seen from
Each view is drawn on the **same** side it is seen from
Projection symbol (a truncated cone in two views)
The circles are to the **right** of the cone's side view
The circles are to the **left** of the cone's side view

blocks.note: Both projections are used: British and European drawings often use first angle, American drawings third angle. Drawings in Jamaica can be either, so always check the **projection symbol**, usually in the title block, before you decide what each view shows.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Edges and holes behind the surface, which cannot be seen from that side, are drawn with **thin dashed lines**. A hole drilled through a block shows as two dashed lines in the side view, with a centre line between them.
When an object has a lot inside it, dashed lines become confusing. A **sectional view** shows the object as if it had been cut through, with the front part taken away.

ul: The **cutting plane** is shown on another view by a chain line, thick at the ends, with arrows showing the direction of viewing and letters, for example A–A.
The view is labelled with the same letters: "Section A–A".
The cut surface is **hatched** with thin lines, usually at 45°, evenly spaced. Different parts touching each other are hatched in different directions.
Holes and hollow spaces are not hatched, so the wall thickness, the depth of holes and the shape of hollow parts are easy to see.

blocks.p: **Centre lines** (thin chain lines) are drawn through the middle of every hole and round part, and along lines of symmetry. Hole positions are dimensioned to their centre lines, so you mark out and drill from them.
A **pictorial** drawing shows an object in three dimensions in one picture, so anyone, including a customer, can understand its shape at a glance.

head: Point
Isometric
Oblique
rows: Upright edges vertical; the other two sets of edges at **30°** to the horizontal, one each way
The front face drawn **true shape**, as seen straight on; depth lines drawn back at **45°** (sometimes 30° or 60°)
True lengths along all three directions
Front face true size; depth either full length (cavalier) or **half length (cabinet)**, which looks more natural
True circles on the front face; put round features at the front
Showing how a part looks or how parts fit; customer sketches; instructions
Quick sketches of objects with one detailed face, such as a gate panel or a box front
Not good for showing every size or hidden detail; circles are harder to draw
Looks distorted if the depth is drawn full length

flow: Draw one vertical line for the nearest corner
From its foot, draw two lines at 30° to the horizontal, one left and one right
Mark the length on one, the depth on the other and the height on the vertical
Draw the other edges parallel to these three directions to complete the box ("crate")
Sketch the shape inside the box, cutting away what is not needed
Go over the visible outlines firmly; erase or leave light the construction lines

ul: Isometric grid paper makes the 30° lines easy.
A sloping edge that does not run along one of the three directions cannot be measured directly: mark its two ends on lines that do, then join them.

blocks.p: A pictorial view is the best way to **show** an idea. An orthographic drawing is the best way to **make** it, because each view shows true shapes and every size, hole and hidden detail can be given clearly. A good sketch for a job often has both: orthographic views with the sizes, and a small isometric view to show the shape.

ul: 1 m = 1000 mm: a length written on a sketch as 2.4 m is 2400 mm on a drawing.
Sizes are in **millimetres** unless a note says otherwise. One note is given ("All dimensions in mm"); "mm" is not written after every number.
**Extension (projection) lines** are thin lines that start a small gap away from the outline and run a little past the dimension line.
**Dimension lines** are thin lines with arrowheads that touch the extension lines. The number sits above the middle of the line, readable from the bottom or the right-hand side of the sheet.
Each size is shown **once only**, so two sizes can never disagree.
Overall length, width and height are always given.
Holes are given as a diameter, with their positions measured to their **centres**.
Outlines and centre lines are never used as dimension lines.
A **leader** (a thin line with an arrow) points from a note to the feature it describes.

head: Method
How
Effect
rows: Each size runs from the end of the last one
Small errors add up along the chain
Every size is measured from one datum edge or line
Errors do not build up from one size to the next: the better choice for hole positions

ul: No part can be made to an exact size, so the drawing says how much each size may vary: its **tolerance**.
"250 ± 1" means any size from 249 mm to 251 mm is acceptable; 251.5 mm is not.
Limits may be written as two sizes, for example 25.0 over 24.8: the part must be between them.
A **general tolerance** in the title block (for example "Unless otherwise stated ±1 mm") applies to every size without its own tolerance.

head: Written on the drawing
Means
Example
rows: Ø12: a hole or bar 12 mm across
R15: a curve of 15 mm radius
Often with their positions or PCD
4 holes at 50 CRS: 50 mm between centres
Typical: the same applies to all similar features
R10 TYP on one corner: all such corners are R10
Sizes given to the CL of a post
CSK hole for a flat-head screw
Above finished floor level / finished floor level

ul: An **arrow** points to the joint; it is joined to a horizontal **reference line** that carries the weld symbol.
A small **triangle** on the reference line means a **fillet weld**; a V shape means a V butt weld. The weld size is written beside the symbol.
A small **circle** where the arrow meets the reference line means **weld all round**.
A small **flag** there means a **field weld**, made on site.
A **tail** at the far end can hold a note, such as the process.
Which side of the line the symbol sits on shows which side of the joint to weld, and the American and ISO systems show this differently: check the drawing, and ask if unsure.

blocks.p: Building drawings are drawn at a reduction scale such as **1:50** or **1:100**. The **floor plan** shows each room from above: walls, doors (with the way they swing), windows, room names and sizes. **Elevations** show the outside walls, and **sections** show the building cut through. Older plans may give sizes in feet and inches.

ul: An electrical **layout plan** is a floor plan with symbols showing where each socket outlet, switch, light, fan, panel and special outlet goes.

The **key (legend)** on the drawing says what each symbol means. Symbols differ between standards (British and IEC symbols look different from American ones), so always read the legend: never guess from the shape.
Thin, often curved, dashed lines from a switch to its lights show **which switch controls which light**, not the cable route.
Mounting heights are given above the finished floor level, for example "Outlets 450 AFFL unless noted". A height written beside one outlet overrides the general note.
Count the symbols of each kind to work out how many boxes, fittings and accessories to order.

head: Diagram
Shows
Does not show
rows: How the parts of a circuit connect electrically, laid out clearly with standard symbols
Where things are in the building, or the real cable routes
Each wire, its colour and the terminal it goes to, often laid out as the equipment really is
The main parts as boxes and how they link, for example supply → meter → main switch → panel → circuits

ul: Window and door openings are often numbered (W1, W2, D1) with their sizes in a **schedule**: use it to count and size burglar bars, grills and gates.
A plan shows the size the opening **should** be. Buildings are not always built exactly as drawn, so measure every opening on site before you cut steel.

blocks.note: Never sketch, measure or open an electrical box or panel that is connected to a supply unless you are trained, authorised and it has been made safe. For sketching practice, use only items the instructor gives you.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **freehand sketch** is drawn by hand without instruments. It need not be to scale, but it must be **roughly in proportion**, so the shape is easy to understand, and it must carry **every size** someone needs to make the item.

ul: Pencils: a 2H for light construction lines and an HB for firm outlines and lettering; an eraser; a sharpener.
Squared grid paper for orthographic views and isometric grid paper for isometric views; a clipboard.
Measuring tools to suit the object: a tape or steel rule for lengths, a **vernier caliper** for thicknesses, small diameters and holes, a protractor for angles.

flow: Study the object; decide which views are needed and which projection you will use
Block in light boxes for each view, in proportion and lined up with each other
Draw the outlines firmly inside the boxes
Add centre lines through holes and round parts, and dashed lines for hidden edges
Measure the object, a feature at a time, with the right tool
Add the dimensions in millimetres, with extension and dimension lines
Add notes: material, thickness, hole sizes, quantity, finish
Add a title, your name, the date, the projection and NTS
Check the sketch against the object: is any size missing?

ul: Judge proportion by comparing sizes: "about twice as long as it is high". Grid squares help: let each square stand for, say, 10 mm.
Draw straight lines in short, light strokes, then firm them up. Turn the paper so you always draw in a comfortable direction.
For a circle, draw a light square first, mark the middle of each side, and curve through the marks.
If the object is worn, bent or broken, measure the undamaged parts and parts that fit with it, and mark any size you had to estimate, so it can be checked.
Customers often send a phone photo of a hand sketch, or a photo of the place. These are a starting point, not a working drawing.
Never take sizes from a photo: the angle and the camera's distance make things look bigger or smaller.
Confirm every size in writing, or measure on site, before anything is made.

blocks.p: A sheet-metal part, such as a tray, a cover with a folded flange or a box, starts as a **flat pattern** (development). Drawing it full size on card, cutting it out and folding it is a cheap way to check the drawing before any steel is cut.

flow: Read the drawing: sizes, flanges, folds, holes
Draw the flat shape full size on card from a datum corner
Draw cut lines as thick continuous lines and fold lines differently (for example thin chain lines)
Mark the holes from their centre lines
Cut on the cut lines with a knife against a steel rule on a cutting mat
Score lightly and fold on the fold lines; tape the corners
Check the model's sizes against the drawing

blocks.note: Cut on a cutting mat, away from your body and the hand holding the rule. Retract the blade every time you put the knife down, pass knives and scissors handle first, and put used blades in the sharps bin.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Title block: right drawing, latest revision, every sheet
Scale, projection symbol, units and general tolerance
Notes and parts list: material, thickness, finish, quantity
Each view: work out the shape, including hidden lines and sections
Dimensions: find every size you need; check that they add up
Ask about anything missing, unclear or contradictory before starting

blocks.h: Making a cutting list from a frame drawing

blocks.p: Look closely at how the corners are made: it changes the cut lengths. Take a rectangular frame 900 mm × 600 mm overall, in 25 × 25 SHS.

head: Corner joint
Long members
Short members
Cuts
rows: 2 at 900 mm (measured long point to long point)
2 at 600 mm (long point to long point)

blocks.p: Write the cutting list as a table: part mark, description, section, length, number needed. Total the length of each section to see how many stock lengths to order, and have the list checked before cutting.

blocks.h: When the drawing and reality disagree

head: Problem
What to do
rows: A size is missing, or the sizes do not add up to the overall size
Read the other views and notes; check the revision; if it is still wrong, stop and ask the supervisor or the person who drew it
You find a mistake on a drawing everyone is using
Tell the supervisor so the drawing is corrected and reissued; do not just correct your own copy
The site does not match the plan (a window is a different size, a wall is elsewhere)
Measure carefully, take a photo and make a dimensioned sketch; report it and wait for a decision
You are given an instruction that changes the drawing
Get it in writing, or a revised drawing; record it with the date and keep it with the job papers

blocks.note: Never guess, and never change a drawing yourself. The supervisor or the person who made the drawing decides, and the change is recorded so everyone works from the same information.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Keep drawings clean, dry and flat, in a folder, a plastic sleeve or a drawing holder, away from water, oil, sparks and hot metal.
Do not fold them small and carry them in a back pocket: they get torn, dirty and unreadable.
Old revisions are removed or clearly marked SUPERSEDED, so nobody uses them by mistake.
Return drawings to their proper place when the job is done.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can name the kinds of drawings and say what each one is for.
I can read a title block: title, number, revision, date, scale, projection, units, tolerance and material.
I can name the A-size sheets and give the size of A4 and A3.
I can say what each type of line shows.
I can work out real sizes from reduction and enlargement scales, and choose a scale for a drawing.
I can explain why I never measure a drawing to find a size.
I can read front, plan and end views in first and third angle projection and recognise the projection symbol.
I can read hidden detail, centre lines and sectional views.
I can read and sketch isometric and oblique views.
I can read dimensions, tolerances, symbols and abbreviations on a drawing.
I can read an electrical layout plan with its legend, and say what circuit, wiring and block diagrams show.
I can measure an object and make a neat, dimensioned freehand sketch of it.
I can work out cut lengths from a frame drawing, allowing for the corner joints.
I can deal with missing sizes, mistakes and site differences, and look after drawings.

terms: A drawing showing how all the parts of a product fit together
A table of each part's name, quantity, size and material
A thin chain line through the middle of a hole or round part
A drawing of one part with all its sizes
The flat shape of a sheet-metal part before it is folded or rolled
A thin line with arrowheads showing the extent of a size
A view of the front, end or side of an object or building
A thin line from the outline showing where a dimension starts or ends
Views drawn on the side opposite to the side they are seen from; plan below the front view
Thin parallel lines, usually at 45°, on the cut surface of a section
A thin dashed line showing an edge that cannot be seen
A 3D view with upright edges vertical and the others at 30° to the horizontal
A floor plan showing where fittings and equipment go
The table on a drawing saying what each symbol means
A 3D view with the front face true shape and depth lines drawn back at 45°
Showing an object as several flat views, each seen straight on
A version of a drawing, shown by a letter or number and a date
The ratio of the size on the drawing to the real size
A view of an object as if cut through, with the cut surface hatched
A drawing made by hand without instruments
Views drawn on the same side they are seen from; plan above the front view
The panel holding the drawing's title, number, revision, scale and other facts
The amount a size may vary and still be accepted
A diagram showing how each wire connects to the terminals of equipment

c1.title: A hinge bracket drawing in Lucea
c1.text: Chevaughn, a trainee at a gate shop in Lucea, Hanover, is given detail drawing HB-07 Rev C of a hinge bracket. The title block says: scale 1:2; first angle projection; all dimensions in mm; general tolerance ±1 mm unless stated; material 8 THK MS plate. The bracket is 160 long and 90 wide overall, with "2 × Ø14" holes and "R10 TYP" on one corner. An end view is drawn to the right of the front view.

c2.title: A customer's phone sketch in Half Way Tree
c2.text: Mrs Bryan, who owns a small office in Half Way Tree, St Andrew, sends a fabrication shop a phone photo of a hand sketch of a window grill, together with a photo of the window. The sketch shows the grill as a 3D picture with its edges drawn at about 30°, labelled "about 4 ft wide". It gives no bar spacing and no height.

c3.title: A salon layout plan in Browns Town
c3.text: Kemoy, an Electrical Installation trainee, is studying the electrical layout plan for a hair salon in Browns Town, St Ann, drawn at 1:100. The note reads "Outlets 450 AFFL unless noted". Most outlet symbols have no height beside them, but the one behind the reception counter is marked 1100. Thin, curved dashed lines run from each switch to some of the light symbols.

c4.title: Copying a pump bracket in Christiana
c4.text: Ackeem must make a freehand sketch of a broken pump bracket at a farm workshop in Christiana, Manchester, so that a copy can be made. The bracket is a bent steel plate with two slots and one round hole; a slot on the back face cannot be seen from the front. One flange has been bent out of shape. Ackeem has a tape, a steel rule, a vernier caliper, pencils and grid paper. He draws his plan view above his front view.

c5.title: A display-stand frame for a Kingston craft market
c5.text: A Kingston fabrication shop is making a display stand for a craft market. The drawing shows a rectangular frame 1200 mm × 900 mm overall in 25 × 25 × 2 SHS, with its corners mitred at 45°, standing on two legs. A sectional view A–A through the frame shows a square with four hatched walls and a clear middle.

questions.q: Chevaughn measures the 90 mm width on the print with a rule and gets 46 mm. What should he work from?
o: 92 mm, from his rule reading doubled
46 mm, the size on the print
90 mm, the written dimension
91 mm, halfway between the two
questions.why: The print may have stretched, or the view may not be drawn exactly to scale. Written dimensions are always used; a measured size is never trusted over them.

questions.q: What does "R10 TYP" on one corner tell Chevaughn?
o: Only that corner is rounded to R10
The corner must be welded with a 10 mm run
The corner is a 10 mm chamfer at 45°
All similar corners are rounded to R10
questions.why: R is radius and TYP means typical: the same size applies to every similar feature, so it is written once instead of on every corner.

questions.q: Chevaughn's finished bracket measures 161.5 mm long. Is it acceptable?
o: Yes, it is within 2 mm of the size
Yes, as the tolerance is ±1 on each end
No, it is more than 1 mm over 160 mm
No, it must measure exactly 160 mm
questions.why: The general tolerance of ±1 mm allows 159 mm to 161 mm. At 161.5 mm the bracket is outside the limit, so it does not meet the drawing.

questions.q: In this first angle drawing, the end view is drawn to the right of the front view. Which end of the bracket does it show?
o: The left-hand end, seen from the left
The right-hand end, seen from the right
The underside, seen from below
The top, seen from directly above
questions.why: In first angle projection each view is placed on the side opposite to the one it is seen from, so a view drawn on the right shows the bracket as seen from its left.

questions.q: Why should the shop not work out the window size from the photo?
o: The photo is too small to measure with a steel rule
Only a drawing at 1:1 can be used to take sizes
It is against the law to measure from a photograph
The camera's angle and distance distort the sizes
questions.why: Things nearer the camera look bigger, and a photo taken at an angle squashes shapes. Only sizes measured on site, or confirmed in writing, can be used to cut steel.

questions.q: What kind of sketch has Mrs Bryan sent?
o: An orthographic plan
An isometric sketch
A sectional view
A wiring diagram
questions.why: A 3D picture with edges at 30° to the horizontal is isometric. It shows the shape well but cannot give the welder every size.

questions.q: Which drawing should the shop make for the welder?
o: A coloured 3D picture of the finished grill, without any sizes
A copy of Mrs Bryan's sketch with "about 4 ft" changed to 1219 mm
A front view with every size, bar spacing, material and quantity
A photo of the window with the grill drawn over it by hand
questions.why: A working drawing needs the true shape and every size: an orthographic view with dimensions, spacing, material and quantity, made from measured or confirmed sizes.

questions.q: On the 1:100 plan, the salon's back wall measures 72 mm. How long is the real wall?
questions.why: At 1:100, multiply by 100: 72 × 100 = 7200 mm = 7.2 m. Use a written dimension if the plan gives one, since prints can stretch.

questions.q: At what height does the outlet behind the reception counter go?
o: 450 mm above the finished floor
1100 mm above the finished floor
1100 mm down from the ceiling level
450 mm above the counter top
questions.why: A height written beside one symbol overrides the general note "unless noted". AFFL means above finished floor level, so this outlet is 1100 mm above the floor, clear of the counter.

questions.q: What do the thin, curved dashed lines from the switches show?
o: Which switch controls which lights
The exact routes the cables must take
Where the walls are to be chased
The position of hidden water pipes
questions.why: Switching lines link a switch to the lights it controls. The cable routes are decided on site or shown on other drawings.

questions.q: Ackeem draws his plan above the front view. Which projection should he write on his sketch?
o: First angle
Oblique
Isometric
Third angle
questions.why: In third angle projection the plan is placed above the front view. The projection must be stated so the reader knows what each view shows.

questions.q: How should Ackeem show the slot on the back face in his front view?
o: With thick continuous lines
With thin chain lines
With thin dashed lines
With hatching at 45°
questions.why: Edges that cannot be seen from the viewing side are drawn as thin dashed hidden lines. Chain lines are for centres, and hatching is for cut surfaces in sections.

questions.q: Ackeem's first sketch looks much longer and thinner than the bracket really is. What should he have done first?
o: Measured every single size before drawing anything at all
Blocked in light boxes in the bracket's proportions
Used a ruler to draw every one of the lines exactly
Drawn it at full size on a larger sheet
questions.why: Light construction boxes, judged against each other ("about twice as long as it is high"), set the proportions before any outline is drawn. A sketch need not be to scale, but it must look like the object.

questions.q: One flange is bent out of shape. How should Ackeem get its sizes?
o: Measure it as it is, since that is the part being copied
Leave the damaged flange off the sketch altogether, as it is bent
Measure undamaged parts and mating holes; mark any estimates
Guess the sizes from what similar brackets usually look like
questions.why: Copying the damage would make a bad part. Sizes from undamaged areas and from the parts it bolts to give the true shape, and marking estimates lets the supervisor check them.

questions.q: With the corners mitred at 45°, what length are the two short frame members, measured long point to long point?
o: 850 mm
900 mm
875 mm
950 mm
questions.why: A mitred member runs the full outside length, long point to long point, so the short members are 900 mm. Only butted members are shortened by the tube width at each end.

questions.q: If the corners were butted instead, with the 1200 mm members running through, what length would the short members be?
o: 850 mm
875 mm
900 mm
questions.why: The short members would fit between the long ones, so 25 mm comes off each end: 900 − 25 − 25 = 850 mm. Always check how the corners are joined before writing the cut list.

questions.q: Section A–A shows a square with four hatched walls and a clear middle. What does this tell the welder?
o: The frame is solid bar
The tube must be cut here
The frame is cut at 45°
The tube is hollow
questions.why: Hatching shows material that the cutting plane passes through; the unhatched middle is empty space. So the section shows hollow tube and its wall thickness.

questions.q: How many A4 sheets are the same size as one A3 sheet?
questions.why: Each A size is half the one above: A3 (297 × 420 mm) cut in half gives two A4 sheets (210 × 297 mm).

questions.q: Leon is starting a neat sketch on grid paper. Which pencil should he use for the light construction lines?
o: A soft 2B pencil
A hard 2H pencil
An HB pencil pressed down firmly
A felt-tip marker
questions.why: A hard pencil such as 2H gives fine, light lines that are easy to erase or leave faint. A softer HB is used afterwards for the firm outlines and lettering.

questions.q: Why are depth lines in a cabinet oblique sketch drawn at half their real length?
o: So the object does not look too deep
So it can be measured directly with a rule
So circles become true ellipses
So it fits the 30° isometric grid
questions.why: Drawn full length (cavalier), the depth looks exaggerated. Halving it makes the sketch look more natural, while the front face stays true shape.
